summary: This RFC updates RFC 5043 and RFC 5044 by extending MPA negotiation for RDMA connection establishment. One enhancement enables peer-to-peer connection establishment, and another adds an option for standardized connection setup.

plainLanguage.summary: Remote Direct Memory Access lets one machine read another machine's memory without copying the data first. Setting that up needs a handshake, and this RFC changes the handshake so that two peers can talk as equals and can agree automatically on how many simultaneous reads each side will allow.

questions: what is enhanced rdma connection establishment
what is ird and ord in rdma
what is an rtr indication in mpa
subtitle: A better handshake for setting up Remote Direct Memory Access, so that neither side has to be the client.

tldr.problem: The MPA handshake used for RDMA over TCP only supports a client-server shape, so peer-to-peer applications have to pretend one side is a server. Two parameters that describe how many remote reads may be outstanding are also left for the application to negotiate by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds four control flags and two 14-bit queue depths to the private data of the MPA request and reply, and adds an explicit Ready to Receive indication so the responder knows when setup is complete.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from April 2012 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 5043 and RFC 5044, and a peer that does not understand it simply closes the connection.

facts.label: Enhanced connection establishment data
facts.value: The first 32 bits of the private data field

facts.label: Queue depth encoding
facts.value: 14-bit unsigned integers, in network byte order

facts.label: Hand the negotiation to the application
facts.value: 0x3FFF, meaning automatic negotiation is not wanted

facts.label: New MPA error codes
facts.value: 0x05 local catastrophic, 0x06 insufficient IRD resources, 0x07 no matching RTR option

facts.value: 512 bytes, with 4 bytes taken by the enhanced data

today: RFC 6581 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2012, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 5043 and RFC 5044 with the new control flags, the queue depth negotiation and the explicit readiness indication, and it adds three MPA error codes and three SCTP function codes to the registries RFC 6580 describes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When used over the Transmission Control Protocol, the Remote Direct Data Placement suite of protocols, defined in RFC 5041, relies on the Marker PDU Aligned Framing protocol of RFC 5044 for both connection establishment and for the markers used for TCP layering.

A typical model for establishing an RDMA connection runs like this. The passive side, the responder, has an upper layer protocol that listens for connection requests. The active side, the initiator, submits a connection request using an RDMA endpoint, the desired destination, and the parameters to be used for the connection, which include RDMA-layer characteristics such as the number of simultaneous RDMA Read requests to be allowed, and application-specific data. The passive side receives that request, which includes the identity of the active side and the requested connection characteristics, and uses it to decide whether to accept and how to create or configure its local RDMA endpoint. If accepting, the responder submits its acceptance, which includes the RDMA endpoint to be used and the connection characteristics, and that generates the accept message to the initiator. The active side then receives confirmation that the connection was accepted, the configured connection characteristics, and any application-supplied private data.

MPA only supports a client-server model for connection establishment, forcing peer-to-peer applications to interact as though they had a client-server relationship. Negotiation of some parameters specific to the Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol of RFC 5040 is also left to the upper layer. Providing an optional upper-layer-independent format for exchanging those parameters would benefit transport-neutral RDMA applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake has always had a shape where one side listens and the other calls. This RFC changes that so either side can call, and adds two numbers to the handshake that say how many reads each side can have in flight at once.

sections.title: Motivations, Read Queue Depths and the Readiness Indication
sections.content:
The goal of the document is two-fold. The first is to extend support from the current client-server model for RDMA connection setup to a peer-to-peer model. The second is to add negotiation of the RDMA Read queue size for both sides of an RDMA connection.

Most RDMA applications are developed using a transport-neutral application programming interface to access RDMA services based on a Queue Pair paradigm, as originally defined by the Virtual Interface Architecture, refined by the Direct Access Programming Library, and most commonly deployed with the OpenFabrics API. These APIs seek to provide a common set of RDMA services whether the underlying transport is, for example, RDDP over MPA, RDDP over SCTP, or InfiniBand.

As currently defined, DDP connection establishment requires the upper layer to encode the RDMA configuration in the application-specific private data. That results in undesirable duplication of logic to cover the RDMA characteristics of both InfiniBand and RDDP for each upper layer, and in a need to specify the extraction of those characteristics for each upper layer. Because both RDDP and InfiniBand support an initial private data exchange, a standard definition of the RDMA characteristics within the private data section would let common connection establishment APIs format those characteristics from the same information used for either protocol.

One of the RDMA operations is an RDMA Read. Read operations are performed using an untagged message sent from a Queue Pair on the local endpoint to a Queue Pair on the remote endpoint, targeting the Inbound RDMA Read Request Queue associated with the connection. Read responses transfer data from the remote endpoint to the local endpoint using tagged messages. An inbound Read Request remains on the queue from the time it is received until the time that the last tagged message associated with it is acknowledged.

One characteristic that must be configured for a Queue Pair is the size of the inbound read queue, called the Inbound RDMA Read Queue Depth. Another is a local limit on the number of simultaneous outbound Read Requests, based on the size of the remote endpoint's inbound queue, called the Outbound RDMA Read Queue Depth. The outbound depth is used to limit the number of simultaneous Read Requests so that the local endpoint does not overrun the remote endpoint's queue. Outbound Reads are submitted to the Send Queue at the local peer rather than to a separate outbound read request queue. Their values are currently left to the upper layer, and because this negotiation is typical, a common mechanism is desirable.

The exchange of MPA Request and Reply messages that places a TCP connection in MPA mode is specified in RFC 5044. It gives the hardware several benefits: the upper layer specifies the exact MPA mode, meaning whether markers and the CRC-32c are enabled, and the point in each TCP stream where MPA frames begin; before the first MPA frame is transmitted all pre-MPA payload has been acknowledged by the peer, so it is never necessary to generate a retransmission that mixes pre-MPA and MPA payload; and before MPA reception is enabled all incoming pre-MPA payload has been acknowledged, so the host never receives a TCP segment that mixes pre-MPA and MPA payload.

The limitation is that the exchange defines no Ready to Receive indication, so the passive side cannot know that the last non-MPA payload, the MPA Reply, has been received. Instead the role of that indication is piggybacked on the first MPA frame sent by the active side. For the classic client-server model this is a valuable optimization, since the client only connects when it has a request to send and the server has nothing to send until it has processed the request. Even a server that sends configuration data immediately can send the same information as application private data in the MPA Reply.

Many peer-to-peer applications, especially those involving cluster calculations, have no natural client or server roles. Typically one member of the cluster is arbitrarily selected to initiate the connection when the distributed task is launched, while the other accepts it. At startup time there is no way to predict which node will have the first message to actually send, and establishing the connections immediately is valuable because it reduces latency once results are ready and validates connectivity throughout the cluster. The lack of an explicit Ready to Receive indication forces all applications to have a first message from the connection initiator, whether or not that matches the application model.

The natural question is why the application layer would not simply generate a dummy message when there is nothing else to send. Three factors make that unsuitable for many peer-to-peer applications. First, transport-neutral APIs: only RDDP over TCP has the first message requirement, while RDDP over SCTP and InfiniBand do not, so an extra message required by only one transport undermines the goal of being transport neutral. Second, work and completion queue accounting: a completion queue must be sized for the possibility that every work request completes in error, and inserting a dummy work request and filtering out its completion would require the lower layer to know the application's usage model and how often an insertion would be required. Third, host-based implementation of MPA fencing: when the generation and reception of MPA frames are already dedicated to hardware, a work completion can only be generated by an untagged message, since the arrival of a message for a tagged buffer does not necessarily generate a completion.
sections.plainLanguage:
The two numbers are the size of the queue that holds incoming read requests and the limit on how many reads may be outstanding. Today each application has to work them out for itself, once for one transport and again for another, and the RFC puts them into the handshake so the same code works everywhere.

The old handshake assumed the caller speaks first, and the responder only learns the caller's side is ready when the first real message arrives. For two peers that is wrong. Sending a dummy message to fill the gap would work, but it would break the promise that the same application code runs over any transport, it would upset the queue sizing the hardware needs, and it would produce a completion that the application did not ask for.

sections.title: Enhanced MPA Connection Establishment
sections.content:
The goal of the enhanced connection setup is to allow standard negotiation of the outbound and inbound read queue depth settings on both sides of the RDMA connection, and to negotiate the initial data transfer operation by the initiator when the existing rule that the client sends first does not match the application requirements.

The RDMA connection initiator sends an MPA Request as specified in RFC 5044, in the new format defined by this document, which allows for standardized negotiation of the two queue depths and for negotiation of the Ready to Receive functionality and the RDMA message type to use for that indication. The responder processes the request and generates an MPA Reply, and the new format completes the negotiation.

The local interface needs to provide a way for an upper layer to request the use of an explicit Ready to Receive indication on a per-application or per-connection basis when one will be required. Piggybacking the indication on the client's first message remains a valuable optimization for most connections.

The RDMA connection initiator must not allow any later frames to be transmitted before the Ready to Receive indication. One method of achieving this is to delay notifying the upper layer that the RDMA connection has been established until after any required indication has been transmitted. All MPA exchanges are performed via TCP prior to RDMA establishment, and are therefore signalled via TCP and not via RDMA completion.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake gains a flag saying which side is which and a flag saying which kind of empty message will be used to signal readiness. Once the reply comes back, the initiator sends that empty message before any real data, and the responder now knows the setup is complete.

sections.title: Enhanced MPA Request and Reply Frames
sections.content:
Enhanced RDMA connection establishment uses an alternate format for MPA Requests and Replies. The 16-byte Key is unchanged, holding the text MPA ID Req Frame for a request and MPA ID Rep Frame for a reply. The M, C and R flags are unchanged. The S flag is new: it is one if the private data begins with the enhanced RDMA connection establishment data, and zero otherwise.

The Res field is one bit smaller than in RFC 5044; otherwise it is unchanged. In RFC 5044 the Res field, in which the newly defined S bit resides, is reserved for future use, and RFC 5044 specifies that it must be set to zero when sending and must not be checked on reception. That is what makes use of the S bit backwards compatible with the original MPA frame format. When the S bit is zero, no additional private data is used for enhanced connection establishment, and the resulting request and reply frames are identical to the unenhanced protocol.

The Rev field contains the revision of MPA. To use any enhanced connection establishment feature it must be set to two or higher. If no enhanced features are desired it may be set to one. A host accepting MPA connections must continue to accept requests with version one, even if it supports version two.

The PD_Length field is unchanged from RFC 5044. It is the total length of the private data field, including the enhanced connection establishment data if present. The private data itself is unchanged, except that if the S flag is set it must begin with the enhanced connection establishment data.

The interoperability rules follow from the S flag. If the responder receives an enhanced MPA message it must respond with an enhanced MPA message. If it receives an unenhanced message, with S set to zero, it must respond with an unenhanced message. If it receives an enhanced message and does not support enhanced connection establishment, it must close the TCP connection and exit MPA; from a standard connection establishment point of view the enhanced frame is improperly formatted, so both sides report TCP connection termination locally. In that last case the initiator may attempt to establish an RDMA connection using the unenhanced protocol if that is compatible with the application, and let the upper layer deal with the queue depths and the peer-to-peer negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The new format is the old one with a single extra bit. If that bit is zero the frame is byte for byte the old frame, so a peer that knows nothing about this RFC sees a normal handshake and answers normally.

sections.title: The Enhanced Connection Establishment Data
sections.content:
Enhanced RDMA connection establishment places 32 bits at the beginning of the private data field of the MPA Request and Reply frames, or of the DDP Stream Session Initiate and DDP Stream Session Accept SCTP Session Control chunks. Upper-layer private data follows this field, so the maximum amount of upper-layer private data is reduced by 4 bytes. The field must be sent in network byte order, with the two queue depths encoded as 14-bit unsigned integers.

The layout is a control flag A for the connection model, a control flag B for the use of a zero-length frame RTR indication, then 14 bits of inbound read queue depth, then a control flag C for the use of a zero-length RDMA Write RTR indication, a control flag D for the use of a zero-length RDMA Read RTR indication, and then 14 bits of outbound read queue depth.
sections.plainLanguage: Four bytes at the front of the private data: two numbers for the queue depths and four one-bit switches, one for the connection model and three for the kinds of empty message that could signal readiness.

sections.title: Negotiating the Queue Depths and the Connection Model
sections.content:
Four terms describe the negotiation. The Initiator IRD is the value sent in the request, the initiator's inbound read queue depth at the time the request was generated. The responder sets its local outbound depth to this value or less, and the initiator IRD is the maximum number of simultaneous inbound Read Requests the initiator can support for the requested connection.

The Initiator ORD is the value in the request. It is the initial value of the initiator's outbound depth and also a request that the responder support a responder IRD of at least this value. It is the maximum number of simultaneous outbound Read operations the initiator wants the responder to support.

The Responder IRD is the value returned in the reply. It is the actual value the responder sets for its local inbound queue depth, and it is greater than or equal to the initiator ORD for a successful negotiation. The Responder ORD is the value returned in the reply, the actual value the responder used for its outbound depth, and it is less than or equal to the initiator IRD for a successful negotiation. After a successful negotiation the responder ORD is at most the initiator IRD and the initiator ORD is at most the responder IRD.

The responder and initiator must pass the peer's provided values to the upper layer as well as using them. The responder outbound depth should be set to a value at most the initiator IRD. If the initiator ORD is insufficient to support the selected connection model, the responder IRD may be increased; for example, if the initiator ORD is 0, meaning the upper layer will not use RDMA Reads, and the responder supports a zero-length RDMA Read RTR indication, the responder IRD can be set to 1. The responder may reject the connection request if the initiator IRD is not sufficient for the required outbound depth, and specify the required value in the reject frame, in which case the termination message must carry layer 2, error type 0, error code 6.

On receiving the accept frame the initiator must set its IRD at least to the responder ORD and its ORD at most to the responder IRD. If the initiator does not have sufficient resources for the required IRD it must send a termination message indicating insufficient resources and terminate the connection, again with layer 2, error type 0, error code 6. The initiator must pass the responder values to the upper layer for both accept and reject messages, and the upper layer can then decide its course of action, for example terminating the connection and renegotiating.

An all-ones value, 0x3FFF, indicates that automatic negotiation is not desired and that the upper layer will be responsible for it. The responder must answer an initiator ORD of 0x3FFF by leaving its local IRD unchanged and setting the IRD to 0x3FFF in its reply, and the initiator must leave its local ORD unchanged on receiving a responder IRD of 0x3FFF. The responder must answer an initiator IRD of 0x3FFF by leaving its local ORD unchanged and setting ORD to 0x3FFF in its reply, and the initiator must leave its local IRD unchanged on receiving a responder ORD of 0x3FFF.

The connection model. Control flag A set to 1 indicates a peer-to-peer model, and 0 a client-server model. Flag B set to 1 indicates that a zero-length frame RTR indication is requested by the initiator and supported by the responder. Flag C does the same for a zero-length RDMA Write RTR indication, and flag D for a zero-length RDMA Read RTR indication. The initiator must set flag A to 1 for the peer-to-peer model, and must set each of flags B, C and D to 1 for each option it supports if flag A is 1. The responder must support at least one RTR indication option if it supports enhanced connection establishment. If flag A is 1 in the request, the responder must set flag A to 1 in the reply. For each initiator-supported option the responder should set the corresponding flag if it can support that option, and it must set at least one option if it supports more than one initiator-specified option. If the responder does not support any of the initiator-specified options it must still set at least one option that it does support.

On receiving the accept frame with flag A set to 1, the initiator must generate one of the negotiated RTR indications. If it cannot generate any of the responder-supported indications it must send a termination message indicating failure to negotiate a mutually compatible connection model or RTR option, with layer 2, error type 0, error code 7. The upper layer can negotiate an upper-layer-level indication when a provider-level one cannot be negotiated.

For the client-server model the initiator must set flag A to 0, the responder must set flag A to 0 if the request has it at 0, and flags B, C and D must also be zero. On reception, if flag A is 0 then flags B, C and D must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side says how many incoming reads it can queue and how many outgoing reads it wants to make, and the reply settles it so that neither side exceeds the other's queue. A value of all ones in either field means the application wants to handle that itself. One control flag says whether this is a two-equal-peers connection or the old request-and-answer one, and three more say which kinds of empty message are acceptable as the readiness signal.

sections.title: SCTP Chunks and Error Reporting
sections.content:
Enhanced RDMA connection establishment uses the first 32 bits of the private data field for the queue depth negotiation in the DDP Stream Session Initiate and DDP Stream Session Accept SCTP Session Control chunks. The type of an SCTP Session Control chunk is defined by a function code. RFC 5043 already defines codes for DDP Stream Session Initiate and DDP Stream Session Accept, which are equivalent to an MPA Request frame and an accepting MPA Reply frame. Three additional function codes are defined here: Enhanced DDP Stream Session Initiate, 0x005; Enhanced DDP Stream Session Accept, 0x006; and Enhanced DDP Stream Session Reject, 0x007. The enhanced reject code must be used to indicate rejection of an enhanced DDP stream session for a configuration that would have been accepted for unenhanced negotiation.

The enhanced DDP stream session establishment follows the same rules as the standard establishment in RFC 5043. Upper-layer private data must be included for the enhanced initiate, accept and reject messages, and must follow the enhanced connection establishment data in the initiate and accept messages. The private data length must not exceed 512 bytes in any message, including the enhanced data, and private data must not be included in the DDP Stream Session TERM message.

Received enhanced DDP stream session control messages should be reported to the upper layer, and any supplied private data must be available for it to examine. A message is not reported to the upper layer if none of the requested RTR indication types are supported by the receiver, in which case the provider may generate a reject reply message indicating which indication types it does support. Enhanced DDP stream management must use the DDP stream session termination function code to terminate a stream established using the enhanced function codes.

On errors, the protocol is layered on RFC 5040 and RFC 5041, and any enhanced connection establishment error generates an MPA termination message. MPA negotiation uses layer 0x2, the LLP error type 0x0 for MPA. RFC 5044 defines four error codes and RFC 5043 defines none, and this document adds three: 0x05 for a local catastrophic error, 0x06 for insufficient IRD resources, and 0x07 for no matching RTR option. That keeps enhanced connection establishment backward compatible with both RFC 5043 and RFC 5044.
sections.plainLanguage: The same negotiation exists for the SCTP version of RDMA, using three new chunk types. When something goes wrong the peers exchange a termination message carrying a code that says which of three things went wrong: something local broke, there were not enough queue resources, or no readiness signal was agreed on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations from RFC 5044 and RFC 5043 apply, and the changes in this document introduce no new security considerations. It is, however, recommended that implementations sanity check the input parameters, including the two queue depths and the control flags used for the RTR indication option negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: No new security rules. The RFC does ask implementations to check the numbers and flags they receive rather than trusting them, since a bad value could cause trouble later.

viz.caption: Why a dummy first message is not a good workaround

items.title: Transport-neutral APIs
items.text: Only RDDP over TCP needs a first message; RDDP over SCTP and InfiniBand do not, so an extra message required by one transport breaks the promise of one application code.

items.title: Queue accounting
items.text: A dummy work request and the filtering of its completion would force the lower layer to know the application's usage model and how often a dummy would be needed.

items.title: Host-based fencing
items.text: When frame generation is in hardware, only an untagged message produces a work completion, so a dummy message creates a completion the application did not ask for.

viz.caption: The enhanced connection negotiation flow described in Section 9.3

messages.label: MPA Request
messages.note: The initiator sets control flag A to 1 for a peer-to-peer model, sets its initial queue depths, and sets flags B, C and D for each readiness indication it supports.

messages.label: MPA Reply
messages.note: The responder matches the flag A value, sets its own queue depths from the initiator's values and the reads the application needs, and sets the flags for the indications it supports.

messages.label: First RDMA message
messages.note: The initiator adjusts its queue depths to the responder's values and sends the negotiated readiness indication. If no indication matches, it sends a termination message instead.

viz.caption: The enhanced connection establishment data at the start of the private data

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Control flag for the connection model. 1 means peer-to-peer and 0 means client-server.

fields.name: B
fields.desc: Control flag for the use of a zero-length frame RTR indication.

fields.name: IRD
fields.desc: Inbound RDMA Read Queue Depth, as a 14-bit unsigned integer in network byte order.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Control flag for the use of a zero-length RDMA Write RTR indication.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: Control flag for the use of a zero-length RDMA Read RTR indication.

fields.name: ORD
fields.desc: Outbound RDMA Read Queue Depth, as a 14-bit unsigned integer in network byte order.

viz.caption: The four values in the queue depth negotiation

cells: The initiator's inbound queue depth sent in the request. The responder sets its local outbound depth to this value or less.
The initiator's outbound queue depth, and a request that the responder support an inbound depth of at least this value.
The inbound queue depth the responder actually sets, at least the initiator ORD for a successful negotiation.
The outbound queue depth the responder actually uses, at most the initiator IRD for a successful negotiation.

viz.caption: The three new MPA error codes

items.label: Local catastrophic
items.desc: A local error was encountered for which no specific error code is defined.

items.label: Insufficient IRD resources
items.desc: The peer's inbound queue depth was not sufficient for the outbound depth the application needs.

items.label: No matching RTR option
items.desc: No mutually compatible connection model or readiness indication could be negotiated.
